moments.title: The Anglo-Saxons arrive
moments.who: Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northern Germany and Denmark
moments.body: After Roman withdrawal from Britain (410 CE), Germanic settlers cross the North Sea. They bring related West Germanic dialects that, over centuries, fuse into Old English. The Celtic Britons retreat westward (Wales, Cornwall) or are absorbed.
moments.takeaway: English starts as a continental Germanic language imposed on a Celtic-then-Latin-then-Celtic substrate. The four main Old English dialects (West Saxon, Mercian, Northumbrian, Kentish) reflect the settlers' kingdoms.

moments.title: Old English literary culture
moments.who: Anonymous scops, Bede, Alfred the Great
moments.body: Beowulf (manuscript dated c. 1000, composition probably earlier) is the longest surviving Old English poem. Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731) is written in Latin but transmits Anglo-Saxon culture. Alfred (r. 871-899) sponsors translation of key Latin works into English and founds an English literary tradition.

quote.text: Hwæt! We Gar-Dena in geardagum / þeodcyninga þrym gefrunon.

moments.takeaway: Old English looks foreign to modern eyes — heavy with case endings, gendered nouns, a vocabulary 95% Germanic. The 'English' you speak today shares much less than half its vocabulary with this.

now.title: Anglo-Saxon survivals
now.body: The 100 most common words in modern English are overwhelmingly Anglo-Saxon: the, of, and, to, in, is, you, that, it, he, was, for. The 'core' vocabulary of family, body, weather, basic verbs (eat, sleep, walk, run, live, die) remains Germanic. Latin and French give the layered, formal vocabulary on top.
now.open_questions: How much of pre-Conquest English do we really know? The textual record is small and skewed (mostly religious, mostly West Saxon). Spoken varieties may have been very different.

items.reflection: Modern English keeps Old English bones inside a French-and-Latin skin. The difference between 'come' and 'arrive', 'kingly' and 'royal', 'house' and 'mansion' is a thousand-year-old social register.

moments.title: The Norman Conquest
moments.body: William defeats Harold at Hastings on 14 October. The English aristocracy is replaced by Norman French speakers. For roughly 300 years, England is trilingual: French for the court and aristocracy, Latin for the church and law, English for the common people.
moments.takeaway: 1066 doesn't kill English — it ranks it. English becomes the language of the conquered.

moments.title: Middle English absorbs French wholesale
moments.body: English borrows around 10,000 French words during this period — government (parliament, justice, court, prison), cuisine (beef, pork, mutton — vs. cow, pig, sheep for the live animals tended by English-speaking peasants), and abstract vocabulary. English also sheds most case endings and complicated gender — possibly accelerated by contact with Norse and French.
moments.takeaway: The Walter Scott observation (Ivanhoe, 1819) about animal/meat names is a real and revealing pattern.

moments.title: Statute of Pleading
moments.body: English is restored as the language of the law courts. Parliament is opened in English in 1362. Chaucer writes The Canterbury Tales (begun c. 1387) in English — and the choice itself is a political statement.
moments.takeaway: English's recovery is incomplete and slow. Latin and French persist in law and church well past 1500.

now.title: A hybrid language
now.body: Modern English vocabulary is roughly 26% Germanic, 29% French, 29% Latin, 6% Greek, and the rest borrowed from everywhere. We have layered synonyms (ask/question/interrogate, kingly/royal/regal) that map onto register. English's openness to loanwords — without an academy to police them — is a Norman inheritance.
now.open_questions: Was Middle English creolised? Some linguists (Bailey and Maroldt, 1977) argued English was a Norse/French/English creole; the mainstream view treats it as heavy contact-induced simplification but not full creolisation.

items.reflection: If you complain about French loanwords in English, you're complaining about a thousand years of English. The hybrid is the language.

moments.title: Caxton sets up shop at Westminster
moments.body: Caxton, who had learned printing in Cologne and Bruges, sets up England's first printing press at Westminster. He prints around 100 books, mostly in English — Chaucer, Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, his own translations. He faces a dialectal decision: which English to use?

quote.text: Loo, what sholde a man in thyse days now wryte, egges or eyren?

moments.takeaway: Caxton tells a story of merchants who couldn't get eggs because the locals didn't recognise the word. He chose East Midlands English (the dialect of London and the university towns) — the basis of modern Standard English.

moments.title: King James Bible
moments.body: The KJV becomes the most influential book in English. Its rhythms, its archaisms (already slightly old-fashioned in 1611), its absorption into common speech — 'the salt of the earth', 'a thorn in the flesh', 'the writing on the wall', 'the powers that be' — shape literary English for four centuries.
moments.takeaway: Together with Shakespeare's First Folio (1623), the KJV gives early modern English a prestigious standard.

moments.title: Johnson's Dictionary
moments.body: Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language' — 42,773 entries, written largely by Johnson alone over nine years — is the most influential dictionary before the OED. It uses illustrative quotations from literature, sets a tone of judicious authority, and helped fix spelling and meaning for the next century.
moments.takeaway: Johnson initially intended to 'fix' the language but came to accept that change was inevitable. The Preface is one of the great essays on lexicography.

now.title: Standard English now
now.body: Standard British English (sometimes 'BBC English' or 'received standard') is a written norm with broad consensus and a much looser spoken norm. American English diverged enough by the 19th century — Webster's 1828 dictionary deliberately reforms spelling (color, theater) and codifies an American standard. Global Englishes (Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean) are now spoken by more people than British and American combined.
now.open_questions: Will English fragment into mutually unintelligible varieties as Latin did into the Romance languages? Probably not, given continuous global media contact — but the question is taken seriously by linguists like David Crystal.

items.reflection: Standard English wasn't decreed; it was selected — by a printer's economic choice, a king's commission, a lexicographer's stamina, and a market of readers.

moments.title: The vowels shift
moments.body: Between roughly 1400 and 1700, English long vowels systematically raised and diphthongised. Middle English 'name' [nɑːmə] becomes Modern English 'name' [neɪm]. Middle English 'house' [huːs] becomes [haʊs]. The shift affected all long vowels in a chain pattern.
moments.takeaway: Otto Jespersen named it the Great Vowel Shift in 1909. The cause remains debated — perhaps social differentiation after the Black Death, perhaps pull or push chain dynamics.

moments.title: Chaucer to Caxton
moments.who: Middle English giving way to Early Modern
moments.body: Chaucer (c. 1400) rhymes that no longer rhyme in modern pronunciation. By Caxton's first English printing (1476), the shift is well under way. Spelling, fixed by print, freezes pre-shift conventions while pronunciation moves on.
moments.takeaway: The mismatch between English spelling and pronunciation owes much to print fixing spelling before the shift completed. 'Knight' was once pronounced with a /k/, a /ni/, a 'gh' /x/.

moments.title: Shift complete
moments.body: By 1700 the major Shift is complete. Subsequent changes include short vowel modifications, the loss of /r/ in non-rhotic accents (England, Australia, NZ), and continuing regional variation. American English largely retains pre-1700 /r/ patterns.
moments.takeaway: The Shift made Shakespeare's rhymes sometimes unfamiliar to modern readers. Original-pronunciation Shakespeare performances (David Crystal and others) bring back many lost rhymes.

now.title: Why English spelling is hard
now.body: Modern English spelling is partly pre-Shift (knight, light, through) and partly post-Shift (-eat in 'eat' vs 'great'). The mismatch is the largest single source of English spelling irregularity. The Shift, print, and the loss of unstressed final -e all contributed.
now.open_questions: Why did English shift its vowels? German didn't. French didn't. Most theories appeal to social factors (postwar migration into London, Black Death demographics, social mobility) without proving the case.

items.reflection: A three-century-long sound change reshaped English. Its consequences — for spelling, for rhyme, for the gulf between written and spoken English — are still with us. The forces that drove it are still partly mysterious.

moments.title: Caxton sets up Westminster press
moments.body: 1476: Caxton, having learned printing in Cologne and Bruges, sets up England's first printing press at Westminster, near the abbey. He prints around 100 books over the next 15 years — Chaucer, Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, Trevisa's translations, his own translations from French and Dutch.
moments.takeaway: Caxton's books were mostly in English (his market was English readers). He had to choose which English.

moments.title: Eggs or eyren
moments.body: 1490: Caxton's prologue to his translation of the Aeneid tells of merchants seeking eggs at a Kentish farm. The wife says she doesn't speak French; she has 'eyren'. The mismatch ('eggs' from Norse, 'eyren' from Old English) illustrates dialectal variation. Caxton chooses the East Midlands dialect of London, court and the universities.

quote.text: Loo, what sholde a man in thyse days now wryte, egges or eyren?

moments.takeaway: Caxton's choice — East Midlands English — became Standard English. The Chancery scribes had been using a similar dialect since 1430s; print confirmed it.

moments.title: Standard hardens
moments.body: Print stabilises spelling over the next century, though variation continues. The Bishops' Bible (1568), the Authorised Version (1611), Shakespeare's First Folio (1623) all helped fix the standard.
moments.takeaway: Standardisation doesn't mean uniformity — early modern English still had massive variation in spelling and grammar. The standard hardened gradually.

now.title: Print's legacy
now.body: Standard English in writing is fairly uniform globally; spoken English varies enormously by region. The written standard's stability owes much to print's lock-in effect. Subsequent technologies (handwriting, typewriter, computer, web, mobile) have not destabilised the written standard in the same way.
now.open_questions: Will digital communication change the standard? Some changes are visible (emojis, txt-speak, internet usage), but the standard remains robust. The institutional infrastructure (schools, publishers, exam boards) reinforces it.

items.reflection: A 1476 commercial decision by a merchant-printer locked in one English dialect as standard. The lock has held for 550 years. Few cultural decisions have been more consequential — or less deliberate.

moments.title: Hampton Court conference
moments.who: James I and English church leaders
moments.body: January 1604: at Hampton Court, James I orders a new English Bible translation. The Puritan delegation (John Reynolds) had proposed it; James saw political advantages — uniting Protestant English speakers behind one text.
moments.takeaway: James's role was decisive. The translation became 'Authorised' because the King authorised it.

moments.title: Six companies translate
moments.body: 1604-1611: 47 scholars worked in six companies at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge. They drew heavily on Tyndale's earlier translation (1525-30), Coverdale's (1535), the Geneva Bible (1560), and the Bishops' Bible (1568). About 80% of the King James Old Testament and 90% of the New Testament are Tyndale's wording.
moments.takeaway: Tyndale was burned for the same project Tyndale's words became canonical. His work shaped subsequent English translation.

moments.title: Published
moments.body: 1611: the Authorised Version is published. Acceptance was gradual — the Geneva Bible (preferred by Puritans, including the Pilgrims) competed for decades. By the late 17th century the King James version had become dominant.
moments.takeaway: The King James Bible's rhythms and phrases — 'the powers that be', 'the salt of the earth', 'to fight the good fight', 'a thorn in the flesh' — entered ordinary English speech.

now.title: A canonical text
now.body: The KJV remained standard for English-speaking Protestants for nearly four centuries. Modern translations (NIV 1978, NRSV 1989, ESV 2001) compete; the KJV remains in use in some traditions. Adam Nicolson's 'Power and Glory' (2003) is a popular history.
now.open_questions: How does the KJV's archaism affect its reading now? Older readers find familiar rhythms; younger readers find it foreign. Most contemporary English Bibles are now in modern translation.

items.reflection: A translation produced by committee in 17th-century England became one of the most influential texts in the history of English. Its impact on the language — on vocabulary, on cadence, on what counts as elevated style — is incalculable. Few books have been more linguistically generative.

moments.title: Shakespeare's lifetime
moments.body: Shakespeare's working career (c. 1589-1613) coincides with one of the periods of fastest expansion of English vocabulary. The early modern English of his time was actively borrowing from Latin and other languages, creating new English compounds, repurposing existing words.
moments.takeaway: Around 1,700 words first appear in the written record in Shakespeare. Whether he coined them or just first wrote them down is debated.

moments.title: Words attributed to Shakespeare
moments.body: Words first recorded in Shakespeare include 'lonely', 'gloomy', 'bedroom', 'eyeball', 'fashionable', 'lacklustre', 'majestic', 'eventful', 'critic', 'submerge', 'invulnerable', 'champion' (verb), 'arouse', 'undress'. Phrases: 'good riddance', 'in a pickle', 'wild goose chase', 'a foregone conclusion', 'all of a sudden'.
moments.takeaway: Shakespeare reflected a language in active expansion. His audiences (largely literate but not university-educated) could follow new compounds and metaphors.

moments.title: First citations in OED
moments.body: When the OED was first being compiled (mid-19th century), Shakespeare's plays were systematically combed for first citations. The Bard's prominence as the most-quoted English author means he gets credited for many words that may have been current colloquially.
moments.takeaway: Modern OED revisions have predated some Shakespeare 'firsts' as the language record has been deepened. The phenomenon is real but somewhat smaller than older accounts suggested.

now.title: Shakespeare's linguistic reach
now.body: Modern productions, schools, the Royal Shakespeare Company, and continuous adaptation keep Shakespeare's English in circulation. His words and phrases are deeply woven into everyday English. Original-pronunciation Shakespeare (David Crystal's work) reveals how different the language sounded.
now.open_questions: Did Shakespeare coin words or record current usage? Both. His position in early modern English is more reflective than radical, but his prominence has fixed his contributions.

items.reflection: One writer in late-Elizabethan and Jacobean London expanded English vocabulary at a rate few others have matched. Whether he invented or recorded these words, his role in fixing them — through subsequent canonical status — has been enormous.

moments.title: Johnson signs contract
moments.body: June 1746: Johnson signs a contract with seven London booksellers for £1,575 to produce an English dictionary. He estimates three years; it took nine. The plan: define words clearly and illustrate them with quotations from canonical English writers.
moments.takeaway: Johnson worked with six amanuenses in his Gough Square house (now the Dr Johnson's House museum). His method was to mark up texts and pass them to assistants to copy out.

moments.title: Dictionary published
moments.body: April 1755: 'A Dictionary of the English Language' is published in two folio volumes. 42,773 entries, 114,000 illustrative quotations. Definitions are sometimes idiosyncratic — 'oats: a grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people' — and sometimes brilliant.

quote.text: Lexicographer: a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge.
quote.attrib: Samuel Johnson, A Dictionary of the English Language, 1755

moments.takeaway: Johnson's Preface is one of the great essays on lexicography. He had hoped to 'fix' the language; by 1755 he conceded that change was inevitable.

moments.title: The dictionary standard
moments.body: Johnson's Dictionary dominated for over a century. The OED began in 1857 (Philological Society); first published 1884 (A); completed 1928. Webster's American Dictionary (1828) — Noah Webster's deliberately American spelling reforms — created a parallel North American standard.
moments.takeaway: Modern lexicography is now data-driven (corpora, search) and continuous. The OED is updated quarterly online.

now.title: Modern lexicography
now.body: Dictionaries now use vast corpora (Oxford English Corpus has over 2 billion words). Computational lexicography catches usage changes faster than ever. Online dictionaries (OED Online, Merriam-Webster) are updated continuously.
now.open_questions: Is the printed dictionary obsolete? Largely yes — the OED's last complete print edition was 1989. The online environment is more flexible and more current.

items.reflection: One man with six assistants and nine years produced the most influential English dictionary before the OED. Johnson's combination of literary judgment, illustrative method and prefatory wisdom shaped what dictionaries do — and how they are read.

moments.title: Philological Society launches the project
moments.who: Richard Chenevix Trench and the Philological Society
moments.body: November 1857: Trench delivers two papers ('On Some Deficiencies in our English Dictionaries') arguing the language needs a comprehensive historical dictionary. The Philological Society commits to producing one. The project takes 70 years.
moments.takeaway: Trench's call for inclusion of all words found in English texts — by historical principles, with dated quotations — defined modern historical lexicography.

moments.title: Murray takes over
moments.body: March 1879: James Murray, a Scottish lexicographer, signs a contract with Oxford University Press for the New English Dictionary on Historical Principles. He builds the famous Scriptorium — a corrugated-iron shed in his back garden — and recruits readers worldwide to send in quotations slips.
moments.takeaway: Murray edited around half the eventual OED himself. Henry Bradley, William Craigie and Charles Onions took over other sections.

moments.title: First edition complete
moments.body: April 1928: the complete first OED is finally published — 70 years after the project began, 49 years after Murray became chief editor (he died in 1915, before completion). Twelve volumes, 414,825 entries, 1.83 million illustrative quotations. The most ambitious lexicographical project ever attempted.

quote.text: We are not adding words to the dictionary, we are merely collecting them.

moments.takeaway: Simon Winchester's 'The Surgeon of Crowthorne' (1998) and 'The Meaning of Everything' (2003) made the story popular.

now.title: The OED today
now.body: Subsequent editions: Supplement (1972-86), Second Edition (1989, integrating supplement), Third Edition (in continuous online update since 2000). The OED Online (subscription) is updated quarterly. Around 600,000 words documented. The continuing project is one of the great achievements of modern scholarship.
now.open_questions: When will the Third Edition be 'complete'? Probably never. The plan is continuous update; finished print editions are unlikely.

items.reflection: A 70-year volunteer project produced the most comprehensive historical record of any language in the world. The OED's combination of historical principle, illustrative quotation and continuous expansion has shaped how every other major dictionary now works.

moments.title: Lowth's Short Introduction
moments.who: Robert Lowth, later Bishop of London
moments.body: 1762: Robert Lowth's 'A Short Introduction to English Grammar' published. The book sets out grammatical rules based partly on Latin (don't end sentences with prepositions, don't split infinitives, double negatives are wrong). Lowth's rules become widely taught.
moments.takeaway: Lowth's grammatical 'rules' often described what scholarly writers should aspire to, not what ordinary speakers actually did. They became prescriptive norms anyway.

moments.title: Murray's English Grammar
moments.body: 1795: Lindley Murray's 'English Grammar' published. It drew heavily on Lowth. Murray's book sold around 16 million copies over the next 50 years — perhaps the most widely-sold English grammar ever. It shaped how generations were taught the language.
moments.takeaway: The split-infinitive rule, the avoidance of 'shall/will' confusion, and the don't-end-with-a-preposition rules trace to Lowth-Murray prescriptivism.

moments.title: Descriptivism takes over linguistics
moments.body: Modern academic linguistics is descriptive — describing how the language is actually used, not how some think it should be. Bloomfield's 'Language' (1933), Chomsky's generative grammar (1957 onwards), and modern corpus linguistics all work this way. Prescriptivism survives in school, publishing and editing, not in academic linguistics.
moments.takeaway: The descriptive-prescriptive distinction is now standard A-level Language teaching. Geoffrey Pullum and others have written widely against prescriptivist 'zombie rules'.

now.title: Living with prescriptivism
now.body: Style guides, school grammar, publishing house styles all maintain prescriptive norms. The split-infinitive and 'preposition at end' rules are widely ignored in modern style but still surface in correction culture. The gap between school grammar and linguistic description remains live.
now.open_questions: Should prescriptivism go? Linguists generally argue yes for academic purposes; publishers and educators often defend it for consistency. The cultural function of 'good grammar' has political and class dimensions.

items.reflection: Two 18th-century grammar books shaped how generations of English speakers were taught their language — and built rules that didn't always match the language they aimed to standardise. The legacy persists in school grammar and editing conventions even as modern linguistics has moved on.

moments.title: American Spelling Book
moments.body: 1783: Webster publishes 'A Grammatical Institute of the English Language' (later 'The American Spelling Book'). The 'Blue-Backed Speller' becomes the standard American school spelling book — over 100 million copies sold over the next century. Webster wanted American English to be distinct from British.
moments.takeaway: Webster was a nationalist. He saw spelling reform as nation-building.

moments.title: Compendious then American Dictionary
moments.body: 1806: 'A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language' — first American dictionary. 1828: 'An American Dictionary of the English Language' — Webster's masterwork, two volumes, 70,000 entries. Spelling reforms: color (not colour), honor, theater (not theatre), check (not cheque), traveled (not travelled), aluminum (not aluminium).
moments.takeaway: Webster's reforms were strategic — he could have gone further (he tried 'tung' for 'tongue', 'wimmen' for 'women' — these didn't stick).

moments.title: Merriam-Webster
moments.body: 1843: George and Charles Merriam acquire Webster's dictionary after his death. They produce successive editions, including the Webster's Third New International Dictionary (1961, controversial for its descriptivism). Merriam-Webster continues as a major American dictionary publisher.
moments.takeaway: Webster's Third (1961) divided opinion — some found it too permissive (it included 'ain't' without disapproval). The descriptivist-prescriptivist debate played out in dictionary reception.

now.title: Two standard Englishes
now.body: American and British written English are now broadly mutually intelligible but distinct in spelling, vocabulary and (to a lesser extent) grammar. Webster's reforms account for much of the spelling difference. Global Englishes (Australian, Canadian, Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean) blend the two standards differently.
now.open_questions: Will the standards converge or diverge further? Mass media keep them mutually familiar; institutional inertia keeps the differences. Convergence on neither is the current state.

items.reflection: An American nationalist's strategic spelling reforms produced one of the two major written standards of English. Webster's combination of scholarly ambition and political project shaped the language across two continents — and his dictionary's descendants still police American English.

moments.title: RP named
moments.body: 1869: Alexander Ellis describes 'received pronunciation' in 'On Early English Pronunciation' — the prestige accent of educated southern England, particularly the public schools. Daniel Jones's 'English Pronouncing Dictionary' (1917) codified it.
moments.takeaway: Earlier prestige accents existed (the court, the educated London speech) but RP became a named variety only in the 19th century.

moments.title: BBC adopts RP
moments.who: John Reith, BBC's first General Manager
moments.body: November 1922: the BBC begins broadcasting. Reith's policy: educated southern English (RP) as the standard for newsreaders and announcers. The Advisory Committee on Spoken English (1926) under Robert Bridges advised on pronunciation.
moments.takeaway: BBC English' became one of the most-heard accents in the world. Many British listeners heard standard southern English daily for the first time.

moments.title: RP's retreat
moments.body: From the 1980s onwards, the BBC actively diversified accents in broadcasting. Regional Britain (Yorkshire, Geordie, Scouse, Welsh, Scots) became normal on national news. RP is now one of many accents heard, though still associated with prestige in some contexts.
moments.takeaway: Estuary English (David Rosewarne, 1984) — a London-influenced accent — has spread across southern England, displacing both Cockney and RP at many social levels.

now.title: Accent in modern Britain
now.body: RP is now spoken by perhaps 2-3% of UK speakers and is increasingly varied within itself (conservative RP, modern RP). Estuary English continues to spread. Multicultural London English (MLE) is a major youth variety with strong influence on British music and media. Class-accent correlation has weakened but not vanished.
now.open_questions: Is RP a class marker or an outdated symbol? Both. Younger speakers from elite backgrounds often modify their RP toward Estuary. The signal value has shifted.

items.reflection: An accent associated with one social class became the standard for a national broadcaster and (through global service) for English-speaking listeners worldwide. The shift in broadcasting from RP to accent diversity is one of the most visible language changes of recent decades.

moments.title: Rosewarne names Estuary English
moments.body: October 1984: linguist David Rosewarne publishes 'Estuary English' in Times Educational Supplement. The article identifies a new accent emerging along the Thames Estuary — mixing features of London (Cockney) with RP. T-glottaling, L-vocalisation, /h/-dropping (sometimes).
moments.takeaway: Rosewarne's coinage caught on rapidly. The accent had been developing for decades; he gave it a name.

moments.title: Estuary spreads
moments.body: Estuary English spreads northward (the Midlands), westward (Bristol), and into broadcasting. Critics worry about loss of regional distinction; defenders point to social mobility and decline of class accent. Tony Blair (PM 1997-2007) used Estuary features in political speech.
moments.takeaway: The accent is associated with youth and informality. It cross-cuts class boundaries that older accents marked.

moments.title: MLE rises
moments.body: Multicultural London English (MLE) — a youth variety drawing on Caribbean, African, South Asian and Cockney elements — has emerged since the 2000s. Spoken by young Londoners across ethnic groups. Strong influence on UK music (grime, drill) and on British youth speech beyond London.
moments.takeaway: MLE has been formally studied by linguists since the early 2000s (Paul Kerswill, Eivind Torgersen, Sue Fox). The future may see MLE features spreading more widely.

now.title: Accents reconfigured
now.body: Modern Britain's accent landscape includes (broadly) RP, Estuary, MLE, urban regional accents (Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle), and various non-urban varieties. The traditional accent map of the early 20th century has been substantially redrawn.
now.open_questions: Will RP disappear? Some linguists predict yes, replaced by a more general modern southern English. The signalling functions of accent shift as social class changes.

items.reflection: Accents respond to social geography. The Thames Estuary and London's multicultural neighbourhoods have become the centres of innovation in British pronunciation in the past 40 years — displacing the public-school RP that defined the previous century's prestige.

moments.title: Martha's Vineyard
moments.body: 1962: Labov's first major study examines the pronunciation of /aw/ and /ay/ on Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts. Local fishermen are showing exaggerated traditional pronunciation as a way of maintaining identity against summer tourists. Linguistic change tracks social identity.
moments.takeaway: The Martha's Vineyard study is one of the founding texts of variationist sociolinguistics.

moments.title: NYC department store survey
moments.body: Labov's PhD research (1962-64, published 1966) on r-pronunciation in NYC. He asks shop assistants in Saks (high-end), Macy's (mid), and S. Klein (working-class) for the location of items 'on the fourth floor'. Repeated to elicit careful and casual styles. The pattern: more /r/ pronunciation in higher-class stores; assistants shift in careful speech.
moments.takeaway: The /r/ variable was a class marker; everyone knew it (the rapid style shift showed this). The result was a foundational finding of modern sociolinguistics.

moments.title: Sociolinguistic methodology
moments.body: Labov's 'Sociolinguistic Patterns' (1972) defined the methodology. Variation by class, gender, age, ethnicity, style is now the framework for sociolinguistic study. Peter Trudgill (Norwich 1974), Penelope Eckert (Detroit high schools, 1989), Peter Patrick and others extended the approach.
moments.takeaway: Labov is one of the most-cited modern linguists. His combination of rigorous quantitative method with social interpretation defined the field.

now.title: Variationist sociolinguistics today
now.body: Modern sociolinguistics has expanded to include ethnographic methods, identity, indexicality (Penelope Eckert's third wave). Studies of MLE, AAE (African American English), regional variation continue. Computational sociolinguistics uses Twitter and other corpora.
now.open_questions: How do social factors and language interact? Modern sociolinguistics has developed nuanced theories — class, gender, race, identity, network — but the core insight (linguistic variation is socially structured) remains Labovian.

items.reflection: One study in Manhattan department stores founded a field. Labov's combination of method, quantitative analysis and social interpretation showed how social structure shows up in everyday speech — and gave linguists tools to study the relationship.

moments.title: The Social Differentiation of English in Norwich
moments.who: Peter Trudgill, University of East Anglia
moments.body: 1974: Trudgill's PhD work, based on a 1968 survey of Norwich, published. Variables include (ng) — pronounced /n/ or /ŋ/ in 'walking' — and others. Results show variation by class, age, gender and style. Working-class men use covert prestige forms (non-standard /n/); middle-class women use overt prestige.
moments.takeaway: Trudgill's study established that gender differences in linguistic variation are real and patterned — women generally using more standard forms than men of the same class.

moments.title: Sex, covert prestige and linguistic change
moments.body: Trudgill's 1972 paper introduces 'covert prestige' — non-standard forms valued within working-class male peer groups. The conflict between overt prestige (standard, middle-class) and covert prestige (non-standard, working-class male) is a major dynamic in sociolinguistic variation.
moments.takeaway: Covert prestige helps explain why non-standard varieties persist despite official disapproval — they carry social meaning users value.

moments.title: Sociolinguistic theory develops
moments.body: Lesley Milroy's Belfast work introduced social networks. Janet Holmes's New Zealand work on gender. Penelope Eckert's 'jocks and burnouts' study (1989) at a Detroit high school showed how identity drives variation. Trudgill's many books on sociolinguistics and dialectology made the field accessible.
moments.takeaway: Modern sociolinguistics is a major branch of academic English. A-level English Language studies its findings regularly.

now.title: Variation now
now.body: Modern variation studies use corpora, social media, and ethnography. Gender variation studies have become more nuanced (Robin Lakoff 1975's framework — 'women's language' — has been substantially critiqued and refined). Penelope Eckert's third-wave sociolinguistics emphasises identity construction over deterministic correlation.
now.open_questions: Why do women use standard forms more than men? Multiple competing explanations: social mobility, judgement of women's speech, identity work, network differences. The pattern is robust; the explanation contested.

items.reflection: A study in Norwich in the late 1960s established core findings of British sociolinguistics. The patterns Trudgill identified — class, gender, style — still organise how variation is studied. Sociolinguistics owes much of its modern shape to this work.

moments.title: Milroy in Belfast
moments.body: 1970s: Lesley Milroy's PhD research in Belfast working-class communities (Ballymacarrett, Clonard, Hammer). She studies linguistic variation through social network analysis — density (do members of a network know each other?) and multiplexity (are ties multiple-stranded — workmate, neighbour, friend?). High-density multiplex networks reinforce non-standard usage.
moments.takeaway: 'Language and Social Networks' (1980, second edition 1987) is one of the major modern sociolinguistic studies.

moments.title: Network theory generalised
moments.body: 1985: 'Linguistic Change, Social Network and Speaker Innovation' (Journal of Linguistics). The Milroys argue innovation spreads through weak ties; strong-tie networks resist change. The implication for language change: change agents are likely to be marginal to dense networks.
moments.takeaway: The application of Mark Granovetter's 'strength of weak ties' (1973) sociology to language change reshaped understanding of how change spreads.

moments.title: Authority in Language
moments.body: 1991: 'Authority in Language: Investigating Standard English' (third edition 2012). The book examines prescriptivism, the ideology of standardisation, and standard language ideology. Influential in sociolinguistic teaching.
moments.takeaway: The Milroys' work bridges variationist methodology and cultural critique of language standards.

now.title: Networks online
now.body: Modern sociolinguistics extends network theory to online communities. Tweet sharing, Instagram comment threads, gaming communities — all create networks where linguistic features spread. The patterns of weak-tie innovation and dense-tie maintenance recur.
now.open_questions: How do digital networks differ from face-to-face? Some patterns recur; others (rapid spread of memes, formation of micro-vernaculars) are new. Modern sociolinguistics is still working this out.

items.reflection: Belfast working-class communities in the 1970s gave sociolinguistics one of its most productive theoretical frameworks. Network theory, weak ties, language change — the Milroys integrated sociology and linguistics in ways that continue to shape both fields.

moments.title: Austin's Harvard lectures
moments.who: J.L. Austin at Harvard William James Lectures
moments.body: 1955: J.L. Austin (Oxford philosopher) delivers the William James Lectures at Harvard. Published posthumously as 'How to Do Things with Words' (1962). The argument: many utterances are not statements but performances — 'I promise', 'I bet', 'I name this ship'. Performatives, not constatives.
moments.takeaway: Austin's distinction between locutionary (saying), illocutionary (doing in saying — promising, ordering), and perlocutionary (effect on hearer) became fundamental to pragmatics.

moments.title: Searle's Speech Acts
moments.body: 1969: John Searle's 'Speech Acts' systematises Austin's framework. Searle later (1975, 'Indirect Speech Acts') develops the analysis of indirect requests — 'Can you pass the salt?' as request, not literal question.
moments.takeaway: Searle's framework became standard in pragmatics. Modern AI work on intent recognition draws on the framework.

moments.title: Speech acts in linguistics
moments.body: Speech act theory was widely adopted in linguistics, sociolinguistics and AI. Conversation analysis (Sacks, Jefferson, Schegloff) developed parallel insights about turn-taking. Cross-cultural speech act studies (Wierzbicka, Blum-Kulka) examined cultural variation.
moments.takeaway: Modern pragmatics is one of the major linguistic subfields. Speech acts are taught in A-level English Language as core concepts.

now.title: Doing with words now
now.body: Online speech acts (memes, hashtag activism), AI assistants (recognising user intent), and political speech all draw on speech act analysis. The framework has been continuously useful since 1962.
now.open_questions: Are all utterances speech acts? Most pragmaticists say yes — even apparently descriptive statements perform acts (assertion, prediction). The framework's generality is part of its power.

items.reflection: An Oxford philosopher's lectures created a field. Speech act theory transformed how language was understood — from description of the world to action in the world. Sixty years later it remains central to pragmatics, AI, and cultural analysis.

moments.title: Grice's William James Lectures
moments.body: 1967: Paul Grice delivers the William James Lectures (published 1989 as 'Studies in the Way of Words'). The cooperative principle: 'Make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange.' Four maxims: quantity, quality, relation, manner.
moments.takeaway: Grice's framework explains how we communicate more than we literally say — through 'conversational implicature'.

moments.title: Logic and Conversation
moments.body: 1975: 'Logic and Conversation' is widely published in Cole and Morgan's 'Syntax and Semantics 3'. The four maxims become standard teaching content. Grice's distinction between what is said and what is meant has organised pragmatics ever since.
moments.takeaway: The maxims are not commands but assumptions. Hearers assume speakers are following them and interpret accordingly. Flouting maxims signals implicature.

moments.title: Neo-Gricean and relevance theory
moments.body: Various successors developed Grice's framework. Stephen Levinson's neo-Gricean pragmatics (2000). Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson's Relevance Theory (1986) replaces maxims with a single principle of relevance. Both shape modern pragmatics.
moments.takeaway: Cross-cultural Gricean studies have shown maxims work differently across cultures — quantity and quality vary; politeness conventions intersect.

now.title: Implicature in everyday life
now.body: Grice's framework is taught at A-level. Modern applications include legal interpretation (what was meant vs said), AI dialogue systems, cross-cultural communication, courtroom evidence. The framework's persistence shows its explanatory power.
now.open_questions: Are Grice's maxims universal? Cultural variation is real but cores of cooperative communication appear robust. The relationship between Gricean assumptions and cultural variation is live in modern pragmatics.

items.reflection: An Oxford philosopher's analysis of how we communicate meaning beyond literal words organised the modern study of pragmatics. Grice's maxims remain in textbooks 50 years later because the phenomena they describe — implicature, indirect speech — are ubiquitous in human communication.

moments.title: Politeness theory
moments.body: 1978 (revised 1987): Brown and Levinson's 'Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage'. They draw on Erving Goffman's notion of 'face' — positive face (desire to be approved) and negative face (desire not to be imposed on). Politeness strategies mitigate face-threatening acts.
moments.takeaway: Brown and Levinson examined cross-cultural data (English, Tamil, Tzeltal) and argued for universal politeness mechanisms with cultural variation.

moments.title: Five strategies
moments.body: 1. Bald on-record ('Pass the salt'). 2. Positive politeness ('Hey friend, pass me the salt'). 3. Negative politeness ('Could you possibly pass me the salt?'). 4. Off-record indirect ('Hmm, no salt over here'). 5. Don't do the FTA at all. Choice depends on social distance, power difference, and ranking of imposition.
moments.takeaway: The framework is widely used in cross-cultural communication training, conflict resolution, and politeness teaching.

moments.title: Beyond Brown-Levinson
moments.body: Critics (Eelen 2001, Watts 2003) argue the framework overgeneralises Western politeness norms. Modern politeness research has moved toward 'discursive' approaches focused on local context rather than universal principles. East Asian face concepts (Chinese mianzi, Japanese kao) don't map exactly onto Brown-Levinson.
moments.takeaway: Politeness research is now pluralistic — Brown-Levinson remains influential but is complemented by alternative frameworks.

now.title: Politeness in practice
now.body: Politeness theory shapes pragmatics teaching, cross-cultural training, customer service training, and online communication etiquette guides. Modern social media has generated new politeness debates (#tone-policing, 'rude' typography, the lost handshake).
now.open_questions: Is politeness universal? Brown-Levinson said yes (with cultural variation in surface); critics say differently in different cultures. The debate continues.

items.reflection: A theoretical framework about how we manage face in interaction has become one of the most-applied frameworks in pragmatics. Brown and Levinson's combination of cross-cultural ambition and theoretical specificity made it teachable, testable and continuously revisable.

moments.title: Syntactic Structures
moments.body: 1957: Chomsky's 'Syntactic Structures' published. Transformational generative grammar argues language structure is innate and rule-governed. The book launches the cognitive revolution in linguistics.
moments.takeaway: Chomsky's framework displaced behaviourist approaches to language within a decade. He remains one of the most influential intellectuals alive.

moments.title: Review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior
moments.body: 1959: Chomsky's devastating review of B.F. Skinner's 'Verbal Behavior' (1957). The review argues behaviourist conditioning cannot explain how children acquire complex language with the 'poverty of the stimulus' — sparse, error-ridden input.
moments.takeaway: The Skinner review is often credited as the moment behaviourism died (in language acquisition theory at least). The 'language acquisition device' (LAD) postulates innate language capacity.

moments.title: Universal Grammar and Principles and Parameters
moments.body: 1965: 'Aspects of the Theory of Syntax' introduces 'competence' vs 'performance'. 1981: 'Lectures on Government and Binding' introduces parameters. 1995: 'The Minimalist Program' simplifies the framework. Universal Grammar — the innate language faculty — remains controversial.
moments.takeaway: Critics of UG (Daniel Everett, Geoffrey Sampson) argue it overgeneralises; defenders argue it explains language universals and acquisition speed. The debate continues.

now.title: Chomsky's legacy
now.body: Generative grammar is one of the dominant traditions in linguistics. Cognitive linguistics (Lakoff, Langacker), construction grammar, usage-based approaches compete. Modern computational linguistics (transformer models) has reopened questions about whether innate structure is necessary or whether sufficient data and architecture suffice.
now.open_questions: Do large language models (LLMs) refute Universal Grammar? Some argue yes — they learn language from data alone. Chomskyans argue they learn statistical patterns, not language.

items.reflection: A single linguist reshaped modern cognitive science, philosophy of mind, and political activism (Chomsky's anti-imperialist politics is another career). His linguistic framework, even where contested, has set the agenda for generations of work.

moments.title: Verbal Behavior
moments.body: 1957: Skinner's 'Verbal Behavior' published. Language is analysed as operant behaviour — verbal responses reinforced by listener consequences. Children learn language through stimulus-response conditioning, with reinforcement shaping correct production.
moments.takeaway: Skinner had built behaviourism into a major psychological framework (the Skinner box, operant conditioning with rats and pigeons). Verbal Behavior was the application to humans.

moments.title: Chomsky's review
moments.body: 1959: Chomsky's review (in the journal Language) attacks Verbal Behavior. The 'poverty of the stimulus' argument: children acquire language faster, more uniformly, and with more abstract structure than reinforcement can explain. The review is widely credited with effectively ending behaviourist accounts of language acquisition.
moments.takeaway: Skinner did not respond directly. The cognitive revolution was under way.

moments.title: Usage-based revival
moments.body: Late 20th and 21st-century usage-based linguistics (Michael Tomasello, Joan Bybee) revived parts of the behaviourist framework, without the strict conditioning model. Children learn language through actual usage, social interaction and frequency — but with strong cognitive and social mechanisms.
moments.takeaway: The debate between innate (Chomskyan) and usage-based approaches continues. Modern positions are usually hybrid.

now.title: Language acquisition now
now.body: Modern language acquisition research includes innate (UG), usage-based, social-pragmatic, and connectionist approaches. Skinner's pure behaviourism is largely abandoned, but operant conditioning principles still inform speech therapy and some teaching methods (autism early intervention).
now.open_questions: What's actually innate? Strong nativism (UG) and pure usage-based learning are both being refined. Most modern theorists accept some constraints on possible languages but argue about how much.

items.reflection: A psychology giant proposed a behaviourist account of language; a young linguist demolished it. The exchange is one of the foundational moments of cognitive science. Both Skinner and Chomsky shaped modern thinking about mind, language and learning — even where they were wrong, their formulations created the questions.

moments.title: Piaget's stages
moments.body: 1920s-60s: Piaget develops a stage theory of cognitive development — sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11), formal operational (11+). Language acquisition is tied to cognitive development; egocentric speech becomes inner thought.
moments.takeaway: Piaget's stages are influential but later research has shown more continuous development than his stage theory predicted. Children often show abilities earlier than Piaget thought.

moments.title: Vygotsky's social development
moments.body: 1920s-30s: Vygotsky develops his own theory — language is fundamentally social, learned in interaction with more capable peers and adults. The 'Zone of Proximal Development' is the gap between what a child can do alone and with help. 'Scaffolding' (Jerome Bruner's later term, 1976) is the support that enables learning.
moments.takeaway: Vygotsky died young (1934) and his work was suppressed in the Soviet Union for decades. He became widely known in the West only after 1960s translations.

moments.title: Modern synthesis
moments.body: Bruner, Wood and Ross (1976) introduce 'scaffolding' as the support that helps a learner achieve more than they could alone — building on Vygotsky. Modern education theory often blends Piagetian and Vygotskyan ideas. Cognitive load theory, sociocultural theory all extend the framework.
moments.takeaway: Modern child language acquisition research (Tomasello, Lieven) draws on both Piaget and Vygotsky alongside contemporary cognitive science.

now.title: Educational application
now.body: Piaget and Vygotsky remain on A-level Language and Psychology syllabuses. Scaffolding is mainstream educational practice. Modern child development research has substantially complicated both stage and social-only accounts. The combined Piaget-Vygotsky synthesis shapes much teacher training.
now.open_questions: How important is interaction vs maturation? The modern answer is both. The relative weighting varies by context, child and theorist.

items.reflection: Two early-20th-century theorists — one Swiss, one Soviet — defined competing accounts of how children develop. Modern child development theory blends and refines them. Their key insights — Piaget's structured development, Vygotsky's social learning — are now mainstream.

moments.title: Language and Woman's Place
moments.body: 1975: Robin Lakoff's 'Language and Woman's Place' published. Lakoff argues women's language is characterised by hedges, tag questions, intensifiers, polite forms, hypercorrect grammar, and 'empty' adjectives ('lovely', 'divine'). The features reflect (and reinforce) women's subordinate social position.
moments.takeaway: Lakoff's account was based partly on introspection and observation rather than systematic data. It opened the field even as later research refined or rejected its specific claims.

moments.title: Tannen's You Just Don't Understand
moments.body: 1990: Tannen's 'You Just Don't Understand: Women and Men in Conversation' becomes a bestseller. The 'difference' approach: women and men use language in different ways (Tannen frames them as different 'cultures'). Critics (Deborah Cameron) argue the framework downplays power asymmetries.
moments.takeaway: Tannen's accessible writing took gender linguistics to mass audiences. Whether it overstates difference is debated.

moments.title: Critique and refinement
moments.who: Janet Holmes, Penelope Eckert, Deborah Cameron, Mary Bucholtz
moments.body: 1992: Holmes's research challenges Lakoff's claims about tag questions (which serve multiple functions). Cameron's 'The Myth of Mars and Venus' (2007) critiques the difference approach. Eckert and McConnell-Ginet's 'Language and Gender' (2003) presents a more nuanced framework.
moments.takeaway: Modern gender linguistics is more contextual — gender is performed, varies by community, intersects with class, race, sexuality.

now.title: Gender in language now
now.body: Gendered linguistic patterns are real but more complex than the early models claimed. Trans linguistic studies, non-binary speakers, the relationship between gender expression and language all expand the field. Online gendered communication has generated its own subfield.
now.open_questions: Do women and men really speak differently? Yes on average and in specific patterns; no in ways that justify deterministic generalisation. Context, identity, situation all matter.

items.reflection: A 1975 book opened a field that has been continuously refined for nearly 50 years. Lakoff's claims have been substantially modified, but the question — how does gender structure language use? — has continued to organise productive research and contested public conversation.

moments.title: Language and Power
moments.body: 1989: Norman Fairclough's 'Language and Power' published. Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) examines how language reproduces and challenges social power. Drawing on Foucault, Halliday's systemic functional linguistics, and Bakhtin, Fairclough analyses texts from political speech, advertising and media.
moments.takeaway: CDA is now a major branch of applied linguistics. Fairclough's three-dimensional framework (text, discourse practice, social practice) is widely taught.

moments.title: Discourse and Social Change, Critical Discourse Analysis
moments.body: Fairclough's subsequent books develop the framework. 'Discourse and Social Change' (1992) and 'Critical Discourse Analysis' (1995) extend the analysis. Ruth Wodak's discourse-historical approach and Teun van Dijk's socio-cognitive approach are parallel CDA traditions.
moments.takeaway: CDA's combination of linguistic analysis and social critique has been embraced by sociolinguists, sociologists, media studies.

moments.title: Critiques and extensions
moments.body: Widdowson and others have criticised CDA for projecting ideological readings onto texts without sufficient linguistic constraint. Defenders argue the framework is sufficiently rigorous when applied properly. Modern CDA extends to multimodal analysis (image, sound) and digital discourse.
moments.takeaway: Modern critical discourse analysis remains a major teaching and research framework — for political discourse, media, business communication and educational analysis.

now.title: Discourse and power
now.body: CDA is taught at A-level and in many university courses. Application to political speech (Brexit, Trump), corporate communications, journalism is continuous. Modern multimodal CDA examines images, videos and social media alongside text.
now.open_questions: Is CDA scientific or political critique? Both, on its own terms. Whether the political stakes are appropriate for the linguistic methodology is contested.

items.reflection: A 1989 book opened the major late-20th-century framework for analysing language and power. CDA's combination of linguistic technique and social critique has shaped how generations of students and researchers approach language in its political dimensions.

moments.title: Categories of the Theory of Grammar
moments.body: 1961: Halliday's 'Categories of the Theory of Grammar' lays the foundation for systemic functional linguistics (SFL). Grammar serves communicative purposes — three metafunctions: ideational (representing experience), interpersonal (enacting relationships), textual (organising the message).
moments.takeaway: SFL is functionally oriented — grammar is what it does. The contrast with Chomskyan generative grammar (autonomous syntax) is fundamental.

moments.title: Introduction to Functional Grammar
moments.body: 1985 (revised 1994, 2004): Halliday's 'Introduction to Functional Grammar' becomes the standard textbook for SFL. The framework is widely taught in Australia, Canada, the UK, China and elsewhere.
moments.takeaway: SFL has been particularly influential in education — content-based language teaching, language across the curriculum, register and genre teaching.

moments.title: Genre, register, multimodal
moments.body: James Martin's genre theory, Hasan's work on cohesion, multimodal extensions (Kress and van Leeuwen). The Halliday-Hasan model of cohesion has shaped how text-level features are taught. SFL is now applied to multimodal analysis (image, sound, gesture).
moments.takeaway: Modern SFL is a major teaching framework in literacy education globally.

now.title: Functional grammar today
now.body: SFL is taught in many university applied linguistics programmes. Its functional orientation makes it useful for teaching, professional communication training, translation studies. Critical discourse analysis (Fairclough et al.) draws extensively on SFL.
now.open_questions: How does SFL relate to other approaches? It is theoretically different from generative grammar but compatible with much pragmatic and sociolinguistic work. Critics argue its categories are sometimes loose; defenders emphasise its practical productivity.

items.reflection: A British-Australian linguist developed an alternative to Chomskyan formalism that has shaped language teaching globally. SFL's focus on what grammar does — rather than just what it is — gives it particular educational utility.

moments.title: Sacks's UCLA lectures
moments.who: Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff, Gail Jefferson
moments.body: 1960s: Harvey Sacks (1935-1975) gives lectures at UCLA on conversation. He records telephone calls (including a suicide hotline) and analyses them in extraordinary detail. The lectures (published posthumously, 1992) are foundational to conversation analysis (CA).
moments.takeaway: Sacks died young (car accident, 1975). Schegloff and Jefferson carried the project forward.

moments.title: A Simplest Systematics
moments.body: 1974: 'A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation' published in Language. The paper analyses how speakers manage turn-taking — without explicit instructions or central coordination. Turn-construction units, transition-relevance places, and a set of rules.
moments.takeaway: The paper is one of the most-cited in linguistics. CA's combination of close empirical observation and systematic analysis is hard to replicate.

moments.title: Institutional and cross-cultural CA
moments.body: CA extends to medical encounters (doctor-patient), courtroom talk, news interviews, classrooms. Cross-cultural CA examines how conversational structures vary across languages. Modern multimodal CA includes gaze, gesture and embodiment.
moments.takeaway: CA is now widely used in applied linguistics, sociology, communication studies. The Conversation Analytic Roundtable and biennial conferences sustain the field.

now.title: Talk as ordered
now.body: Conversation analysis has shown that what looks like chaotic talk is highly organised. Modern CA continues to extend to new domains — telemedicine, online video chat, AI assistants. The methods are continuous: detailed transcription, sequence analysis, careful description.
now.open_questions: What does CA explain? Critics argue it describes patterns without explaining them; defenders argue description at this level is itself explanation of a sort.

items.reflection: A series of UCLA lectures founded the field that takes everyday conversation seriously as an organised social activity. CA's methodological rigour and empirical depth have made it one of the most distinctive 20th-century contributions to language study.

moments.title: Three concentric circles
moments.body: 1985: Braj Kachru proposes the three-circles model. Inner circle: native English-speaking countries (UK, US, Canada, Australia, NZ). Outer circle: post-colonial nations where English is widely used (India, Nigeria, Pakistan, Singapore). Expanding circle: countries using English as foreign language (China, Japan, much of Europe).
moments.takeaway: Kachru's model legitimised the study of 'World Englishes' as varieties rather than imperfect approximations of British or American English.

moments.title: World Englishes as field
moments.body: Edgar Schneider's 'Postcolonial English' (2007) proposes a dynamic model of how new Englishes develop through phases. The journals 'World Englishes' (1985) and 'English Today' (1985) institutionalise the field.
moments.takeaway: By 2024, around 1.5 billion English speakers — only around 380 million native. Most English is now used between non-native speakers.

moments.title: ELF and decolonisation
moments.body: English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) research examines how non-native speakers communicate effectively with each other. Decolonising debates extend to questions of which English to teach. Indian English, Nigerian English and others are now valid teaching targets in their own right.
moments.takeaway: The 'standard' English of educated native speakers is no longer the only legitimate teaching model.

now.title: Global English now
now.body: Modern global English is increasingly multilingual at the system level — most speakers code-switch or speak multiple varieties. The dominance of US English in technology is balanced by the demographic weight of Indian and Nigerian English. World Englishes is a major branch of modern English studies.
now.open_questions: Will global English fragment into mutually unintelligible varieties? Most current evidence says no — written English maintains a strong core; mass media keep spoken varieties broadly accessible.

items.reflection: An Indian-American linguist legitimised the study of English's many varieties as varieties — rather than imperfect approximations of one ideal. Kachru's model reshaped how global English is studied, taught and valued.

moments.title: Language and the Internet
moments.body: 2001 (revised 2006): David Crystal's 'Language and the Internet' is the first major linguistic survey of online language varieties — email, chat, web, instant messaging, virtual worlds. Crystal argues internet language is a new medium with its own conventions, not a degraded form of standard English.
moments.takeaway: Crystal's calm assessment — txting and the internet are not destroying language — countered moral panic of the period.

moments.title: Txtng: The Gr8 Db8
moments.body: 2008: Crystal's 'Txtng: The Gr8 Db8' examines text messaging. Findings: txtng abbreviations are smaller proportion of texts than feared; texters know standard English; texting may improve literacy by increasing writing practice. The book defends txt-speak against critics.
moments.takeaway: Crystal's empirical approach grounded popular debates in actual data. Most predictions of language decline have not materialised.

moments.title: Social media linguistics
moments.body: Gretchen McCulloch's 'Because Internet' (2019) is a major popular survey. Modern internet linguistics examines memes, gif use, emoji, the new genre of one-word responses. The internet has developed its own conventions of tone (sarcasm marking, capitalisation for emphasis, all-lowercase casual).
moments.takeaway: Internet linguistics is now a real subfield. Its findings: digital language is mostly creative adaptation, not decline.

now.title: Language online today
now.body: Modern English language A-level includes online language study as standard content. The continuous evolution of platform-specific conventions (Twitter/X, TikTok, WhatsApp, Discord) keeps the field current. AI-generated text raises new questions.
now.open_questions: How does AI change online language? Large language models produce massive amounts of text. The relationship between AI output and human language is now central to applied linguistics.

items.reflection: Linguists have responded to digital communication with empirical study rather than moral panic. The findings — language adapts, conventions develop, change is normal — provide a useful framework for thinking about technological change in communication.

moments.title: William Jones identifies Indo-European
moments.body: 2 February 1786: William Jones's address to the Asiatic Society. Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and other languages share a 'common source... no longer perhaps existing'. Comparative philology and the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European begin.
moments.takeaway: Jones's insight launched modern historical linguistics. The Indo-European language family — covering most of Europe, Iran and northern India — has been one of the major intellectual reconstructions.

moments.title: Grimm's Law
moments.body: 1822: Grimm identifies the systematic sound change from Proto-Indo-European to Germanic languages. PIE *p > Germanic f (Latin pater, English father); PIE *t > Germanic θ (Latin tres, English three); PIE *k > Germanic h (Latin cor, English heart). Sound change is regular.
moments.takeaway: Grimm's Law was foundational. The Neogrammarian principle — sound change is exceptionless — has been refined but remains powerful.

moments.title: Causes of change
moments.body: Modern theories of language change include: internal (assimilation, simplification of unusual structures), external (contact, borrowing), social (covert prestige spreading non-standard forms), prestige imitation. Most changes have multiple causes.
moments.takeaway: Change is constant. English has been changing rapidly for 1,500 years and continues to do so.

now.title: Current change
now.body: Modern English changes observable in real time: 'literally' as intensifier (centuries old, currently expanding); 'like' as discourse marker (since 1980s); 'because + noun' ('because reasons'); 'they' as singular non-binary pronoun (rapidly accepted since 2010s).
now.open_questions: Are some changes irreversible? Most are. Some prescriptive rules hold off changes (split infinitives) for decades; eventually the standard usually catches up with general usage.

items.reflection: Language change is one of the most rigorously documented natural processes. The 200-year history of historical linguistics gives us tools to see English's continuing change as part of a long pattern — not decline, not chaos, but constant evolution.

moments.title: First BBC broadcast
moments.body: 14 November 1922: the BBC begins broadcasting from 2LO in London. Daily news, music, talk. Audience: any household with a wireless set. Reith establishes 'inform, educate, entertain' as principles. Newsreaders use RP — Received Pronunciation.
moments.takeaway: Within a decade, millions of British households were hearing standard educated southern English daily. The accent's reach was unprecedented.

moments.title: Wartime broadcasting
moments.body: WWII: BBC becomes essential — radio sets the national mood. Wilfred Pickles (Yorkshire) is given news-reading shifts partly to make it harder for German broadcasters to fake BBC broadcasts. The first regional accent on national news.
moments.takeaway: The BBC's wartime role cemented its place in British culture. The English the nation heard was deliberately calibrated.

moments.title: Accent diversification
moments.body: From the 1980s, the BBC actively diversifies accents. Regional UK accents become routine on national news. International English (Australian, American, South Asian) appears regularly. The 'BBC accent' is no longer one accent.
moments.takeaway: The shift mirrors broader cultural change in Britain. Class accents are less rigid; regional pride is greater.

now.title: Broadcasting English
now.body: Modern UK broadcasting features a much wider accent range than 1922-80s. The BBC's pronunciation department continues to advise on words. Internet streaming, podcasts and social media now compete with traditional broadcasting as language-norm influences.
now.open_questions: Has broadcasting lost its standard-setting role? Partially. Social media and streaming services now have comparable reach. The BBC remains influential but is no longer dominant.

items.reflection: A century of broadcasting shaped how English-speakers around the world heard one variety of English. Its current decline as monolithic standard-setter is itself a major shift in how language norms work — and is largely a consequence of broadcasting's earlier success in normalising standardisation.

moments.title: First SMS
moments.body: 3 December 1992: Neil Papworth, a Vodafone engineer, sends the first SMS to Richard Jarvis on his Orbitel 901 — 'Merry Christmas'. Text messaging is born. Within a decade it is the dominant non-voice communication method for billions.
moments.takeaway: Early SMS was limited to 160 characters. The constraint drove abbreviation conventions — 'gr8', 'ur', 'lol', 'omg'.

moments.title: Moral panic
moments.body: 2000s: tabloid press warns that 'txt-speak' is destroying English. John Humphrys's 'I h8 txt msgs' (2007) was a typical example. The fear: a generation unable to write standard English.
moments.takeaway: The fear was largely unfounded. Most research (Plester, Wood, Bowyer, Crystal) shows texting does not damage literacy; some shows it improves spelling sensitivity.

moments.title: Smartphones and changing patterns
moments.body: Smartphones (from 2007) ended the 160-character constraint. Texting moved from abbreviation-heavy to fuller language. WhatsApp, iMessage, Signal, Telegram now carry most personal messaging. Emoji (Unicode standardised 2010) have replaced some text abbreviations.
moments.takeaway: The conventions changed once the underlying constraint changed. Linguistic creativity adapts to medium.

now.title: Mobile language now
now.body: Modern texting uses fuller orthography than peak SMS era. Emoji, GIFs, voice notes, video supplement text. Different platforms develop different conventions. Generational differences (Gen Z's all-lowercase casual, Boomer texting conventions) are visible.
now.open_questions: How does multimedia change communication? Voice notes, video calls, emojis all expand what 'messaging' is. The boundary between text and other media has blurred substantially.

items.reflection: A medium's constraints shape its conventions. SMS conventions tracked its limits; modern smartphone messaging tracks its different ones. Predictions of linguistic decline rarely come true because language responds to its uses faster than its commentators can keep up.

moments.title: Cheshire's Reading study
moments.body: 1982: Cheshire's 'Variation in an English Dialect' studies Reading adolescents. Non-standard 'I done' and 'I seen' are produced more by male peer-group members. The study confirmed gender, group identity and youth as variation factors.
moments.takeaway: Cheshire's work was foundational to British sociolinguistic study of youth varieties.

moments.title: Multicultural London English emerges
moments.who: Paul Kerswill, Jenny Cheshire and team
moments.body: MLE — Multicultural London English — described by Kerswill, Cheshire, Torgersen, Fox in a series of papers from 2007. A new ethnically-neutral youth variety drawing on Caribbean, African, Cockney and other sources. Spoken by young Londoners across ethnic backgrounds.
moments.takeaway: Features include monophthongal /eɪ/, 'man' as pronoun, GOOSE-fronting, distinctive 'th'-stopping. The variety has spread beyond London.

moments.title: MLE in music and media
moments.body: MLE became audible globally through UK grime (Skepta, Stormzy), drill, and viral social media. Young speakers across the UK pick up features through media exposure. The conservative defence of 'proper English' continued in commentary; the language continued to change.
moments.takeaway: Modern variety spread happens partly through media. MLE is a striking example of language change driven by youth, ethnicity and pop culture.

now.title: Multilingual modern Britain
now.body: MLE is now a major focus of UK sociolinguistic research. Its emergence has been compared to earlier multi-ethnic urban varieties (New York English in the 1930s-50s, Brazilian Portuguese in São Paulo). The patterns recur where multilingual urban populations interact intensively.
now.open_questions: Will MLE spread further? Some features have spread beyond London (West Midlands, Manchester, Glasgow). Others remain concentrated. The medium-term trajectory depends on demographic and cultural factors.

items.reflection: Multilingual London produced a new English variety in real time. The combination of Caribbean, African and indigenous London influences, mediated through youth culture and music, has created one of the most studied recent varieties of English. The process — bottom-up, multi-ethnic, youth-led — is a model for understanding contemporary language change.

moments.title: Ecclesiastical History
moments.body: 731: Bede completes 'Ecclesiastical History of the English People' (Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum) in Latin. Five books, dictated to scribes — including the story of Cædmon (the first English poet according to Bede), the conversion of Northumbria, and a chronology that helped establish the AD dating system in northern Europe.
moments.takeaway: Bede wrote in Latin but recorded much about the development of English-speaking culture. His translations included Old English versions of parts of John's Gospel (now lost).

moments.title: Alfred's translations
moments.body: 871-899: King Alfred the Great commissions translations of major Latin works into Old English — Gregory's Pastoral Care, Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Augustine's Soliloquies. Alfred himself participates in the translation programme. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle begins around 890.
moments.takeaway: Alfred treated literacy in English as foundational to good government. His programme made Old English a serious literary language.

moments.title: Old English literary culture
moments.body: 9th-11th c.: Old English literary culture develops — Beowulf, The Dream of the Rood, The Wanderer, The Battle of Maldon, Ælfric's homilies. By the time of the Norman Conquest, England has the most developed vernacular literary tradition in Europe.
moments.takeaway: The Norman Conquest set this back — English ceased to be the language of administration and high culture for 300 years.

now.title: Old English now
now.body: Old English is taught at university level. Modern English speakers can recognise some Old English vocabulary (hus = house, mann = man, scip = ship) but the grammar (cases, conjugations, word order) is foreign. Tolkien's Anglo-Saxon scholarship shaped his fiction and reshaped popular interest in the period.
now.open_questions: What did Old English really sound like? Reconstructed pronunciations (David Crystal and others) give approximations. The texts give us the language scribes wrote; spoken varieties may have differed.

items.reflection: Pre-Conquest English had a richer literary culture than most of Europe. The Conquest's interruption — three centuries of French dominance in administration — makes the survival of English itself in those years one of the major facts of English language history.

moments.title: Chronicle begins
moments.body: c. 890: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is begun, probably under King Alfred's patronage. It compiles earlier annals and continues them. Multiple manuscripts (Parker A, Cotton B, C, D, E, F, G) reflect copies sent to different monasteries that updated independently.
moments.takeaway: The Chronicle was kept up at different monasteries for centuries — the longest at Peterborough, where entries continued until 1154.

moments.title: The Conquest in the Chronicle
moments.body: The Chronicle's account of the Norman Conquest is one of the earliest English-language sources. Domesday Book (1086) is described: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land... which was left out.' The Chronicle records the Conquest from the perspective of those who lived it.
moments.takeaway: The 1066 entry contains some of the most vivid English-language reporting from a contemporary.

moments.title: Final entry
moments.body: 1154: the Peterborough manuscript's final entry. The Chronicle has been continuously kept for 264 years. The 'Anarchy' under King Stephen is movingly described — 'Men said openly that Christ slept, and his saints.'
moments.takeaway: By 1154 the language has shifted toward early Middle English. The Chronicle's last entries reflect the gradual transformation.

now.title: First continuous English prose
now.body: The Chronicle is the longest continuous English-language historical document. Modern editions (Susan Irvine's recent edition of MS E, the multiple-manuscript ASC project) make it accessible. It is foundational for both linguistic and historical study.
now.open_questions: Whose voice speaks in the Chronicle? Annals from different monasteries reflect different local perspectives. The 'national' chronicle is in fact a regional patchwork.

items.reflection: Three centuries of continuous English-language record-keeping survived through the Norman Conquest and beyond. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is unique in early medieval Europe — both as historical source and as the longest continuous tradition of vernacular prose in any European language.

moments.title: French wave
moments.body: 1100-1500: English borrows around 10,000 French words during the Middle English period. Government (parliament, justice, court, prison), cuisine (beef, pork, mutton vs cow, pig, sheep), abstract concepts (liberty, society, religion). Layered synonyms form (ask/question/interrogate, kingly/royal/regal).
moments.takeaway: The Norman wave shaped English's massive vocabulary and register layering. English still has more synonyms than most languages because of these layered borrowings.

moments.title: Latin and Greek wave
moments.body: Renaissance: scholars borrow heavily from Latin and Greek for new concepts. Educate, encyclopedia, atmosphere, sceptical, paradox, irony, sympathy. Inkhorn controversy (mid-16th c.) — were these borrowings necessary?
moments.takeaway: Inkhorn critics (Cheke, Wilson) argued for plain English; the Latinisers won. Many supposedly difficult words from this period are now mainstream.

moments.title: Global English borrowing
moments.body: Modern English borrows from many languages: tsunami (Japanese), karaoke (Japanese), feng shui (Chinese), tikka (Punjabi), kindergarten (German), schadenfreude (German), pizza (Italian), tortilla (Spanish), maverick (Spanish via cowboy English), kayak (Inuit), shaman (Tungus via Russian). Globalisation accelerates the process.
moments.takeaway: English is one of the most receptive of languages to loanwords. The combination of cultural openness (no language academy) and global reach drives continuous expansion.

now.title: Vocabulary now
now.body: Modern English has around 1 million words counting technical and specialist vocabulary. Most are borrowed at some level. The dictionary grows by hundreds of words per year. Tracking new borrowings is one of lexicography's main jobs.
now.open_questions: Is English a creole? Some linguists (Bailey, Maroldt) have argued yes — heavy contact-induced restructuring. Mainstream view treats it as exceptional contact-induced simplification but not strictly creolisation.

items.reflection: English's openness to loanwords is its defining feature. Many European languages have institutional defenders against borrowing (Académie française); English has none. The result is one of the world's richest vocabulary stocks — and one of the most ambivalent relationships to its own borrowings.

moments.title: Words that have shifted
moments.body: Examples: 'nice' (Latin nescius — ignorant; then foolish; then precise; then pleasant). 'Awful' (full of awe; then awesome; now negative).
