'Silly' (Old English sælig — blessed; then innocent; then weak; now foolish). 'Knight' (Old English cniht — boy, servant; then elevated). 'Hussy' (housewife; then disreputable woman).
moments.takeaway: Words change meaning continuously. The trajectory is sometimes amelioration (improving), sometimes pejoration (worsening), often shift in scope.

moments.title: Modern semantic shifts
moments.body: Modern examples: 'literally' (literal; now intensifier). 'Decimate' (kill one in ten; now devastate). 'Sick' (ill; now also impressive). 'Wicked' (evil; now also great). 'Gay' (cheerful; now homosexual; now also pejorative in some youth slang). Each shift is contested by purists.
moments.takeaway: Modern semantic change is observable in real time through corpora. The complaints of pedants are themselves data — they often signal which words are currently shifting.

moments.title: Meaning shift theorised
moments.body: Theories of semantic change: metaphor (mouse for computer device), metonymy (the White House for the US executive), generalisation (dog originally a specific breed), specialisation (deer originally any animal), euphemism/dysphemism cycles.
moments.takeaway: Lexical change is one of the fastest forms of language change. Phonology shifts over centuries; vocabulary can shift in years.

now.title: Meaning under continuous change
now.body: Modern dictionaries (OED quarterly updates) track new meanings. The lag between popular usage and dictionary inclusion has shortened in the digital era. Words like 'cancel' (cancel culture), 'woke', 'gaslight' have all gained new meanings rapidly.
now.open_questions: When is a word's meaning 'real' enough to record? Lexicographers use frequency and durability thresholds. Some changes are ephemeral; others persist.

items.reflection: Meaning is the most fluid feature of language. The same word's meaning can change in a generation. Tracking these changes is one of the most interesting tasks of linguistics — and one of the most contested areas of usage debate.

moments.title: Atlantic pidgins
moments.body: 16th-19th c.: Atlantic pidgins emerge as contact languages between European traders, African slaves, and indigenous populations across the Caribbean and Americas. Pidgin English (multiple varieties), Pidgin French. Children born to pidgin-speakers grow up speaking creoles — pidgins that have become first languages.
moments.takeaway: Modern English-based creoles include Jamaican Patois, Tok Pisin (Papua New Guinea), Hawaiian Pidgin, Krio (Sierra Leone), Belizean Creole, Bislama (Vanuatu).

moments.title: Bickerton's bioprogram
moments.body: Bickerton's 'Roots of Language' (1981) argues creoles reflect a 'language bioprogram' — innate language structures that emerge when children create a full language from limited pidgin input. The framework was challenged but raised important questions.
moments.takeaway: Creole genesis remains debated. Substrate (from contributing languages), superstrate (from dominant language) and universal cognitive constraints all play roles.

moments.title: Creole as language
moments.body: Modern attitudes: creoles are recognised as full languages, not 'broken' versions of English or French. Jamaican Patois has been proposed for official recognition in Jamaica. Translation programmes — including a Patois Bible (New Testament 2012) — extend recognition.
moments.takeaway: Creole speakers often have political battles for educational recognition — the languages have been treated as substandard rather than as full systems.

now.title: Creoles now
now.body: Millions speak English-based creoles globally. Patois has substantial cultural reach through reggae, dancehall and global Caribbean culture. The recognition of creoles as full languages — not deficient varieties — has been a major sociolinguistic achievement.
now.open_questions: Is creole status politically protected? Education policy in many Caribbean countries still privileges Standard English. The debate continues.

items.reflection: Language contact between unequal speakers produced some of the most distinctive language varieties on Earth. The recognition of creoles as full languages — late and incomplete — is one of the major postcolonial linguistic achievements.

moments.title: English Dialect Society
moments.body: 1873: English Dialect Society founded. Joseph Wright's 'English Dialect Dictionary' (1898-1905) — six volumes — documents English dialects before they were extinguished by mass education and broadcasting. Wright had been a wool-mill worker in Yorkshire before becoming Oxford's Professor of Comparative Philology.
moments.takeaway: Many of the dialect words Wright recorded are now lost. The dictionary is a snapshot of regional English in the late 19th century.

moments.title: Survey of English Dialects
moments.who: Harold Orton and Eugen Dieth, Leeds
moments.body: 1950-61: Survey of English Dialects — older rural informants surveyed across 311 sites. Maps showing isoglosses (dialect boundaries) for sounds, vocabulary, grammar. The basic Linguistic Atlas of England (1978) presented the findings.
moments.takeaway: The Survey caught the last generation of speakers using traditional rural dialects. By 2000 many of these dialects had been largely lost.

moments.title: BBC Voices, dialect tourism
moments.body: 1990s-2000s: BBC Voices project, the Sound Comparisons project, and others document modern UK English variation. Urban dialects (Geordie, Scouse, Yorkshire, Brummie, Bristol, Cockney, MLE) thrive while rural dialects continue to fade.
moments.takeaway: Modern variation is partly urban, partly regional, partly generational. The traditional rural dialect map has been substantially replaced by an urban-centred one.

now.title: British dialects today
now.body: Modern UK dialect study uses crowdsourced data, BBC archives and corpora. Major modern varieties: RP, Estuary, MLE, Geordie, Scouse, Manchester, Yorkshire, Welsh English, Scottish Standard English, varieties of West Country, East Anglian. Each has distinctive sounds, words and grammar.
now.open_questions: Are dialects converging or holding? Both. Some features spread nationally (T-glottaling); others remain regional. The 'levelling' thesis (dialect convergence) has been complicated by continuing regional pride.

items.reflection: Britain has one of the densest dialect maps in the world relative to its size. Centuries of relatively stable local communities preserved varieties that mass media have only partly homogenised. The continuing study of variation reveals language responding to social, economic and technological change.

moments.title: The Language Instinct
moments.body: 1994: Pinker's 'The Language Instinct' published. The popular synthesis of Chomskyan generative linguistics with evolutionary psychology. Argument: language is an evolved cognitive capacity, not a cultural invention; UG is real; children acquire language because they are biologically equipped to.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's accessible writing reached audiences far beyond linguistics. The book made nativism the popular mainstream of language science.

moments.title: Words and Rules
moments.body: 1999: Pinker's 'Words and Rules' examines past tenses — both regular ('walked') and irregular ('went') — to argue for a dual-mechanism model. Rules generate regulars; words store irregulars. The framework became a standard reference in psycholinguistics.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's combination of empirical work and popular synthesis defined a generation of cognitive science writing.

moments.title: Debates and dissent
moments.body: Critics: Tomasello, Goldberg and others argue usage-based learning suffices without UG. Daniel Everett's work on Pirahã has been used to argue against language universals (controversial). The debate continues; most positions now accept some constraints and some learning.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's nativism remains influential but is not unchallenged. Modern child language research is more pluralistic.

now.title: Cognitive linguistics now
now.body: Modern cognitive linguistics includes generative grammar, usage-based approaches, neurolinguistics, evolutionary linguistics. Large language models (GPT et al.) raise new questions about how much innate structure language requires. Pinker himself has moved toward broader cognitive science popularisation.
now.open_questions: How much of language is innate? Modern consensus accepts that learning bias and architecture are needed; pure tabula rasa learning seems insufficient. The exact division remains contested.

items.reflection: A 1994 popular book defined how a generation thinks about language in cognitive science. Pinker's argument — that we have a language faculty as a biological inheritance — remains influential, and continues to be tested by new linguistic and computational evidence.

moments.title: Sapir and Whorf
moments.who: Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf
moments.body: 1929-40: Edward Sapir (Yale anthropologist) and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf (fire insurance inspector by trade, amateur linguist) develop what becomes known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis. Language shapes thought — speakers of different languages see the world differently. Whorf's work on Hopi was particularly influential.
moments.takeaway: Strong version: language determines thought (linguistic determinism). Weak version: language influences thought (linguistic relativity).

moments.title: Decline of strong Whorf
moments.body: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 'Basic Color Terms' (1969) appears to refute strong Whorf — colour terms across languages show universal patterns. Cognitive universalism dominates for decades. The strong hypothesis is widely abandoned.
moments.takeaway: Whorf's specific claims about Hopi tenseless thought were also factually disputed. The popular 'Eskimo have 100 words for snow' became an academic cautionary tale.

moments.title: Whorfian revival
moments.body: 1990s-present: 'neo-Whorfian' research finds subtle but real effects of language on thought. Lera Boroditsky's experiments (spatial framing, gender of objects). Stephen Levinson's work on spatial concepts. Daniel Casasanto's work on metaphor. Weak Whorfianism is now respectable.
moments.takeaway: Modern consensus: language doesn't determine thought, but it shapes habitual attention and ease of certain cognitive tasks.

now.title: Language and cognition now
now.body: The relationship between language and thought is one of the active research areas in modern cognitive linguistics. Studies of bilinguals, time perception, spatial cognition, agency attribution, gender all show subtle Whorfian effects. The 'how does it think differently?' question has matured.
now.open_questions: Are Whorfian effects real or just attentional? The line between perception, conceptualisation and habitual attention is hard to draw. Most modern researchers accept effects on attention while remaining sceptical of strong perceptual claims.

items.reflection: An anthropologist and his amateur student proposed that language shapes thought. The strong version of their hypothesis was largely discredited; the weak version has been substantially supported by modern research. The question — how does language shape cognition? — remains live.
